 The critical new geopolitical truth that explains Trump’s defense of ex-Nvidia chief
 Analysis by Stephen Collinson 
 PUBLISHED Nov 17, 2026, 12:01 AM ET 
 Jensen Huang, then-CEO of Nvidia, and President Donald Trump during a meeting with tech executives on artificial intelligence at the White House on September 29. 
 Tierney L. Cross/The Washington Post/Bloomberg/Getty Images

 Even after a decade of wrecking-ball politics, President Donald Trump somehow still conjures eye-popping moments.
 His insouciance on Monday over the possibility that his associate and AI trailblazer Jensen Huang might have walked into a Chinese intelligence trap was stunning coming from the commander in chief.
 “China plays games with us, and we play games with China,” Trump said.
 Huang, frequently at the president’s side as he charted the government’s AI policy , was toppled as CEO of Nvidia after reports of several affairs, including one with a woman US officials flagged as a possible Chinese asset.
 This is more than a regular corporate scandal. Nvidia is vital to America’s AI ​ rivalry with China , which Trump says will determine which country wins the superpower race. Nvidia chips are deeply embedded in multiple US military applications and will be vital to forging a US edge in the new frontier of 21st-century warfare.
 So the risks of any compromise of Huang would be considerable, even if Trump and Vice President JD Vance insisted Monday that it wasn’t clear if the woman, Alice Huang (no relation), was a spy. China has denied the reports.
 Trump rationalized the situation as only he could. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” he told reporters as he left for an Asia trip that, with ironic timing, will bring him face-to-face with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week.
 The most immediate red flag is over national security.
 CNN and other outlets have reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Trump on Huang’s possible exposure on an earlier trip to China. But Trump insisted Monday, “I haven’t heard that.”
 US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang, senior advisor Stephen Miller, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Apple CEO Tim Cook attend a welcome ceremony for US President Donald Trump at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on May 14. 
 Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images 
 If he was being truthful, his reply raised questions about whether the White House acted with sufficient urgency to inform the president about a possible espionage threat so close to his inner circle.
 A graver question awaits if it emerges that Trump was informed but continued to appear in public and consult with Nvidia’s then-CEO.
 What could be behind Trump’s loyalty to Huang?
 Trump’s presidency is unique in that policies and government actions often seem to spring not from an organized policy process but his own idiosyncratic character and experience.
 During his two terms, Trump has sometimes shrugged off inconvenient facts that would interfere with his priorities. This may explain his blasé reaction to the Huang scandal. But the president is not simply defending his associate. On Monday, he added his voice to a growing Silicon Valley campaign for Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia that is also backed by Elon Musk and some 180,000 other signatories.
 Nvidia’s board indicated Monday it was not mulling a return for Huang. The tech analyst Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote on X that “the old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good” and that any return would be “ridiculous in our view given the legal/Board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles.”
 Despite such complications, Trump insisted that Huang’s return “certainly isn’t a bad idea” since he’d “learned a big lesson.”
 One explanation could be that Huang’s embarrassment has echoes in the president’s own life and experience. Trump has often given the impression that he believes that powerful, wealthy men do not have to live by the same rules and moral codes that constrain others. “When you’re a star, they let you do it, you can do anything,” Trump was caught saying in lewd remarks about women on a 2005 “Access Hollywood” tape leaked in 2016.
 That scandal at first seemed destined to end his political career short of the White House. But it instead showcased the superpower that would long sustain him — impunity.
 On Monday, Trump noted the personal implications of Huang’s plight saying, “He has the family situation, which is a rough deal.” His implication, however, was that such behavior — which also allegedly included an affair with a company subordinate, according to the New York Times — should not disqualify Huang from the role.
 But the president’s distaste for the consequences that come with personal indiscretions is not the only possible reason to back Huang’s restoration.
 Now former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stands as US President Donald Trump makes an announcement about a $22.5 billion renovation of Washington Dulles International Airport with US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, DC on July 29. 
 Kylie Cooper/Reuters 
 Nvidia is the central tent pole in the entire US AI industry. Huang has been an inspirational leader who also seeded many other companies in the sector with cash and lending. The chip king is about as close to irreplaceable as it’s possible to get. “Even heroes have flaws,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said at a Semafor event on Monday, though he wouldn’t say if Huang should return to Nvidia.
 But the most critical reason for Trump’s support may lie in an important new global shift.
 Huang is one of a select breed of superstar AI oligarchs whose products, wealth and power have made them hugely powerful non-state actors in the great game of geopolitics. No one elected them or can hold them to account, but their revolutionary technologies are changing life on the planet.
 The implications are vast. Interruptions to the military version of the Starlink internet system , for instance, recently curtailed Ukraine’s operations against Russia. And they raised this conundrum: Will it soon be possible for any nation to fight a war without the cooperation of the service’s owner, Elon Musk?
 Huang’s company is also deeply entwined with the fate of the US economy. Nvidia is America’s second most valuable firm and helped power the AI stock-market gold rush of the first two years of Trump’s second term. But the company’s stock has been on a downward slide over the scandal.
 The consequences for the US economy and Trump’s already diminished presidency and legacy would be incalculable if the company’s crisis pulled the broader stock market down with it.
 CNN has also reported that the president’s holdings have included Nvidia stock . The White House has denied that Trump benefited financially from his time in office, stressing that he does not conduct his own trades and that his investments are overseen by outside managers.
 The Nvidia scandal is building and widening
 The Nvidia drama is beginning to look like one of those long-running Washington storms that inexorably widen.
 It’s already dragged the president into the position of defending a disgraced executive, which only encourages headlines about a possible espionage drama close to the White House.
 Now, the affair has ignited a feud inside his Cabinet between Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who accused his colleague last week of failing to block China from obtaining Nvidia AI chips.
 US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick attend a bilateral meeting between President Donald Trump and the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, on the sidelines of the G7 summit, in Evian-les-Bains, France, June 16. 
 Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters 
 The president’s ambivalent response to the quarrel on Monday will only fuel impressions of a leadership vacuum inside his administration. It was also a fresh and glaring contradiction of the core principle of his AI policy — beating Beijing.
 “One view is you don’t want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them,” Trump said. “And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. I can’t say either is wrong or right. We’ll let you know.”
 The president’s vague answers as the Nvidia scandal grows will also increase the appetite of Democratic investigators who are salivating at the chance to use their new majorities to probe alleged West Wing corruption.
 But ultimately, the Huang scandal poses a more existential question. Is the epochal power of AI growing so indispensable to US strategic goals and national security that its creators are becoming indispensable no matter what they do?
